title: Nan: The Constance Darcy Douglas Story

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: Sutton
chapters.html:
My grandmother’s story begins with her grandmother, in Brome County, Quebec. Julie Deslières was born there in November 1868. She later gave her birthplace as Sutton.

Her parents were married on November 25, 1867, at the mission church of St-Étienne at Bolton, a few months after Célina turned twenty. The register calls the groom Édouard Bonvouloir, a day laborer and still a minor, the son of the late Édouard Bonvouloir and of a mother named Brunelle, of Brome Corner. Bonvouloir was the family’s second name; in later records they are Deslières and Delaire. The bride was Célina Dufresne, also a minor, the daughter of Bazile Dufresne, a day laborer, and Françoise Rotichaud (the surname is hard to read in the register). Her father stood beside her as a witness, and Célina signed her own name. The 1901 census gives her birthday as May 27, 1847.

In the spring of 1871 the census of Canada found her in the township of Bolton, two years old, in the house of her father, Edward, who was thirty-four, and her mother, Celina, twenty-four. There was a baby sister, five months old, also named Celina. The family was French in origin and Catholic.

Twenty years later the 1891 census found the same family at Brome. Edward was forty-three. His ages do not agree from record to record: a minor (under twenty-one) at his marriage in 1867, thirty-four in 1871 as indexed, and forty-three in 1891. Nine children were living at home. Julie, the eldest, was twenty-two, single, and could read and write. The census also records where each parent was born. Edward was born in Quebec. Celina was born in the United States.

On January 9, 1892, in the parish church of St-André at Sutton, the priest married Julie to Thimothée Deslières, a day laborer. The register names his parents as the late Eugène Deslières and Anastasie Bédard, and hers as Édouard Deslières and Célina Dufresne. Both bride and groom were of age and both belonged to the parish. The banns had been read three times. The groom’s brother, François Deslières, stood as a witness. The bride signed her name Julie Delaire, the spelling the family would carry into New England.

Eugène was the name of Thimothée’s father. Two years after this wedding a daughter would be born and named Eugenie. Eighteen years after that, Eugenie would give the same name to my grandmother as her middle name.

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: Jewett Street
chapters.html:
Julia, as she was now known, came to the United States on or about October 30, 1899. She crossed by rail on the Canadian Pacific line and entered at Newport, Vermont. She later swore to those details herself in a federal court in Providence.

By June 1900 she was a widow. The census found her at 53 Jewett Street in Providence, in the house of her sister-in-law, Mary Lague, forty-four, and Mary’s three daughters. Also living there were Mary’s mother, recorded as Enesta C. Delier, sixty-six, and Julia’s own daughter, Eugenia, five. Julia, thirty-one, worked as a cook and had been employed all year. She could read, write and speak English.

On April 28, 1902, Julia married again. The Providence register records the groom as Delphis Noreu, forty-two, a machinist born in Canada and a widower, the son of Charles and Louise. Julia gave her age as thirty-three and her parents as Edward and Selina Delaire. It was a second marriage for both. A Catholic priest, L. O. Massicotte, married them. The marriage did not last long in the records: by 1910 the census again calls her Julia Delaire, a widow.

Ten years later Julia was the head of her own household in Ward 4 of Providence, a widow of forty with her daughter Eugenie, fifteen. She told the census she had borne one child and that the child was living. She was working as a nurse for a private family. It was the first time a record called her a nurse. It would not be the last time that word appeared in this family.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: Oldham and Lowell
chapters.html:
Constance’s English line starts in a Catholic church in a Lancashire mill town. On June 26, 1862, at St. Patrick’s in Oldham, Atkinson Nodders married Mary Regan. The parish register, kept in Latin, names his father as James. The civil index records the same marriage in the Oldham district that spring.

Mary later told a census taker she came to America in 1862, the year of her wedding. The couple settled among the mills of Lowell, Massachusetts. A daughter, Sarah Ann, was born there on April 10, 1863. A second daughter, Mary Ellen, was born in 1867 and died at Lowell on May 28, 1868, a little over a year old.

Margaret Jane Nodders, Constance’s grandmother, was born at Lowell on February 25, 1869, and baptized there on March 9. What became of her father is not yet found in any record.

On December 23, 1869, at Peterborough, New Hampshire, a Mary Regan married. The groom was James H. Stewart, twenty-two, a mill spinner born in Scotland, son of a Scottish innkeeper. Mary gave her age as twenty-six, her birthplace as England, and her father as John Regan, a brick mason born in England. A justice of the peace, Ezra M. Smith, married them.

The marriage card does not mention a first husband or a child, so it does not by itself prove this bride was Margaret’s mother. Several records point that way: the name Regan, an English birth, an age that fits, and a widow named Mary E. Stewart who later lived with Margaret as her mother-in-law. Some details do not fit: in 1910 Mary Stewart said her father was born in Ireland, while the bride’s father was born in England. In June 1880 the census found a James Stewart, born in Scotland, his English wife Mary and a daughter Margaret, ten, born in Massachusetts, in Fall River. A Sarah, seventeen, was in the same household, and two years later Margaret’s sister, Sarah Ann Nodders, married Charles C. Imhoff in Fall River. The ages in that household do not fit perfectly. When Margaret married John F. Darcy in 1888 the register gives her name as Nodders, but the name Stewart turns up again: in 1930 her son-in-law gave her maiden name as Stewart.

In 1910 and again in 1915 the census found Mary E. Stewart, a widow in her late sixties, living in John and Margaret Darcy’s house in East Providence. She told the 1910 census she had borne seven children and that three were still living.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: Borden Street
chapters.html:
The Irish side of the family begins with a blacksmith. In July 1860 a census taker in the fifth ward of Providence wrote down a household he spelled Dorsey: John, thirty, a blacksmith born in Ireland; Catherine, thirty-one, marked as married within the year; Patrick, fifteen; Johanna, ten; Catherine, five; William, three; and a baby, John, seven months old. The baby fits John Francis Darcy, whose late-life records give his birth as December 8, 1859; earlier records disagree, since the 1900 census gives December 1862 and his marriage registers give ages that point to 1861 or 1862.

On June 1, 1875, the Rhode Island census found a Darcy family in the same ward that is very likely the same household, though the ages do not line up neatly: the children are thirteen or fourteen years older, John Sr. ten years older and Catherine only seven. The census taker wrote the name Darcy. John, forty, was still a blacksmith, born in Ireland. His wife Catherine, thirty-eight, also Irish-born, kept house; the census marked her as unable to read or write. Their daughter Catherine, nineteen, was a spooler in a cotton mill. William, sixteen, was a laborer. John, fifteen, was already working as a jeweler.

By June 1880 the father was gone. The census found Catharine Darcy, sixty, a widow, keeping house at 76 Borden Street. Her son William, twenty-two, had become a blacksmith like his father. John F., nineteen, worked for a jeweler.

A Providence savings-bank book from May 28, 1872, holds an account for a John and Catherine Dorcy, husband and wife, both fifty, both born in County Tipperary. Catherine signed with her mark. The record does not prove these are the same couple, but it is the only paper so far that names an Irish county.

On April 17, 1884, John Francis Darcy, twenty-three, a jeweler, married Ellen Elizabeth Winter, twenty-one, born in Ireland, the daughter of Matthew and Mary. A son, Joseph Edward, was born the next spring. He died at five Bogman Street on October 2, 1885, at six months; the register gives teething and convulsions. Two months later, on December 7, 1885, Ellen died of consumption at 78 Borden Street. She was twenty-three.

On January 13, 1888, John married again. The Providence register gives him as twenty-six, a jeweler, the son of John and Catherine, and his bride as Margaret Nodders, nineteen, born in Lowell, Massachusetts, the daughter of Henry and Mary. Patrick F. McKenna, a Catholic priest, married them. The register calls it a first marriage for both.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: The Printer’s Son
chapters.html:
Constance’s father came from the other side of the family entirely. Albert Blake Darcy was born on November 20, 1888, in East Providence; the town’s birth register lists him under the name Darcey, son of John F. Darcey, a jeweller born in Providence, and Maggie, born in Lowell, Massachusetts. His father, John Francis Darcy, was the son of John Darcy and Catherine Fanning. His mother, Margaret Jane Nodder, had been born on February 25, 1869, in Lowell, Massachusetts. Her death certificate names her parents as William Nodder, an Englishman, and Mary E. Regan; her marriage register names her parents as Henry and Mary. John and Margaret were married in Providence on January 13, 1888. The birth registers of East Providence record their children: Albert, November 20, 1888; Lauretta, August 19, 1890, at Rumford; Lillian, August 6, 1892, who married Peter John Barry in 1914; Mary Stuart, September 18, 1895; Harold Francis, April 22, 1898; and Olive Rose, November 6, 1901. No birth registration has been found for Ethel Marguerite; her death certificate gives August 3, 1896, and the 1900 census November 1894. When Ethel died in 1930, her husband gave her mother’s maiden name as Margaret J. Stewart, born at Lowell. On Margaret’s own death certificate in 1942, with Albert as informant, it is Nodder.

In June 1900 the family rented a house at 62 Orchard Street in East Providence. John, a street-railway conductor by then, had been married twelve years. Margaret, thirty-one, had borne six children and all six were living: Albert, eleven; Loretta, nine; Lillian, seven; Ethel, five; Mary, four; and Harvey, two. The census recorded that both of Margaret’s parents were born in England, and both of John’s in Ireland.

Albert went into the newspaper trade and stayed in it. Over the years the records call him a printer, a compositor and a linotype operator, working for the Pawtucket Times and later the Providence Journal.

On January 16, 1912, in Providence, he married Eugenie Emma Delaire. The marriage record gives her age as seventeen, her birthplace as Sutton, Quebec, and her parents as Timothy and Julia M. Delaire. William Pyne officiated.

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: Born on Smith Street
chapters.html:
Constance Eugenie Darcy was born on Saturday, October 12, 1912, at 410 Smith Street in Providence. She was her parents’ first child. The city’s birth register gives her father as Albert B., twenty-three, a printer born in East Providence, and her mother as Eugenia E. Delaire, eighteen, born in Canada.

The house on Smith Street held three generations. The Providence directory for 1913 lists Julia Delaire, widow, boarding at 410 Smith Street, under the same roof as her daughter, her son-in-law and the baby who would become my grandmother.

chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: Alma Street
chapters.html:
A brother, Albert Norman Darcy, was born on December 7, 1915, in Taunton, Massachusetts. The Taunton directories place the young family at 112 School Street in 1915 and at 721 Bay Street in 1916 and 1917. When Albert registered for the draft in June 1917 he was working for the Pawtucket Times. On his card he listed the people who depended on him: his wife, two children and his mother-in-law.

By 1918 Albert was a linotype operator for the Evening Times, living in Providence. In January 1920 the census taker found the Darcys renting at 19 Alma Street in Ward 3 of Providence; the census index misreads it as Alms Street, but the directories for 1919, 1922 and 1923 all print Alma. Albert, thirty-one, was a compositor in a newspaper office. Eugenie, twenty-five, gave French as her mother tongue. Constance was seven and in school. Her brother was four. By 1922 Eugenie was working too, as an upholsterer at 291 Westminster Street.

Julia was by then living on her own on Esten Street, still working as a nurse. In May 1924, at fifty-five, she went before the clerk of the United States District Court and declared her intention to become a citizen. The declaration describes her: five feet tall, 165 pounds, brown hair, brown eyes, a medium complexion. She was living at 46½ Park Street. She signed it Mrs. Julia Delaire.

In April 1925 the Rhode Island census found Albert, Eugenie and the two children at 29 Burgess Avenue in East Providence. Constance was twelve. Listed just before them on the same page was another Darcy household, John J. Darcy, forty-three, and his wife Margaret E.

chapters.label: Chapter 8
chapters.title: Pratt Street
chapters.html:
Constance’s parents did not stay together. By 1927 the Providence directory lists Eugenie on her own, as Mrs. Eugenie E. Darcy, on Evergreen Street, and in 1929 at 19 State Street. On August 1, 1929, Albert took out a license in Brooklyn, New York, to marry Theresa B. Sullivan.

In April 1930 the census found Eugenie, thirty-five and divorced, at the head of her own household at 111 Pratt Street in Providence. She paid twenty-eight dollars a month in rent and had no radio. She was working as an interior decorator for a rug maker. The directories for 1930 and 1932 call her an estimator at 716 North Main Street, living at 41 State Street and then 64 Bridgham Street. Albert, by then, was a compositor at the Providence Journal and lived at Edgewood, and later at Shawomet in Warwick with Theresa. Constance was seventeen and still in school. Albert Norman was fourteen.

Julia was living alone at 31 Wayne Street. She was sixty-one and still gave her occupation as nurse for a private family. She died in Providence on June 15, 1931, and was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston, in section 5, lot 84. She was the first of the family laid in that lot. Sixty-three years later Constance would be buried beside her.

chapters.label: Chapter 9
chapters.title: Westminster Street
chapters.html:
In 1934 the Providence directory listed Constance E. Darcy as a student, rooming at 7 Beacon Avenue; on the line beside her is her mother, Mrs. Eugenie E. Darcy, at the same address. In 1935 her mother was at 35 Dartmouth Avenue. She finished high school. The 1940 census records the highest grade she completed as the fourth year of high school.

By January 1936 she had a trade. A Rhode Island census card dated January 6 of that year gives her address as 75 Abbott Street and answers both the question of her usual occupation and her present one with the same word: hairdresser.

The directory for 1937 placed her at work in room 506 at 290 Westminster Street, in the heart of downtown, and rooming at 11 Grand View. The address was the Lapham Building, an office block at the corner of Westminster and Mathewson Streets that held several beauty shops. Another hairdresser, Catherine V. Hanley, was listed in the same room that year. In 1938 the directory printed her workplace as 290 Wash, room 402; Anton’s beauty shop, run by Anton Kienast, was in room 402 of the Lapham Building and living at 56 Dartmouth Avenue with her mother and brother. She was still at Dartmouth Avenue in 1939. By 1940 her mother had moved to 325 Sayles Avenue in Pawtucket. A block away, on Weybosset Street, a young Scotsman named Lawrence Douglas was dressing store windows.

chapters.label: Chapter 10
chapters.title: Birmingham
chapters.html:
In 1939 a daughter was born in Attleboro, Massachusetts. She was named Eugenie Elizabeth.

On Monday, October 9, 1939, three days before her twenty-seventh birthday, Constance married Laurence in Birmingham, Alabama. The Jefferson County license gives her address as 454 Broadway, Providence, and her parents as Albert B. Darcy and Eugenie Delaire. Thomas R. Lea, a judge of the municipal court, married them.

Sources and record notes

chapters.label: Chapter 11
chapters.title: Valencia Street
chapters.html:
By April 1940 they were in San Francisco. The census found them renting on Valencia Street for thirty-three dollars a month; the census gives no house number. Laurence was a window trimmer in retail clothing; he had worked forty-eight hours in the week before the census, and had earned $2,240 the year before. Constance was keeping house. The census taker first wrote the little girl’s name as Joan, then corrected it above the line to Eugenie.

In October 1940, when Laurence registered for the draft at 129 Julian Avenue, he named Constance as the person who would always know where to find him. In June 1941 the two of them crossed back into the United States from Canada at Blaine, Washington, by stage, bound for home in San Francisco. The immigration card records Constance as an American citizen.

A second daughter, Constance Anderson, was born. By February 1943 Laurence had gone east to the Pittsburgh district with Bond Stores. In his naturalization petition there he named Constance as his wife and listed both girls.

Back in Rhode Island, Constance’s grandmother Margaret Jane Darcy died at her son Albert’s house in Warwick on September 10, 1942.

chapters.label: Chapter 12
chapters.title: Magill Street
chapters.html:
By 1945 they were back in Rhode Island. From 1945 through 1949 the Pawtucket directory lists Laurence and Constance at 97 Magill Street. A third daughter, Norma, was born. By 1950 they had moved to 148 General Street in Providence, and from 1956 they lived at 644 River Avenue.

Those years took two of the men in Constance’s life. Her brother, A. Norman Darcy, had married at Framingham, Massachusetts, in 1938; in 1940 he and his wife, Claire, were renting at 110 Beach Avenue in Warwick with a baby daughter, and Norman, a parking-lot attendant, had worked sixty-five hours in the week before the census. He died on October 1, 1954, at thirty-eight, and was buried in his grandmother Julia’s lot at Saint Ann. Her father, Albert, died on November 4, 1957, sixteen days short of sixty-nine, and was buried at Mount Saint Mary Cemetery in Pawtucket.

chapters.label: Chapter 13
chapters.title: The Nurse
chapters.html:
Constance became a nurse, as her grandmother Julia had been. She trained at the Rhode Island School of Practical Nursing. By 1961 the Providence directory listed her as a nurse at Roger Williams General Hospital.

Laurence died on March 9, 1961, at St. Joseph’s Hospital, at fifty-three. The Pawtucket Times named his wife, Constance, and their three daughters among his survivors. Constance was forty-eight.

In the 1961 directory her mother, now Mrs. Erickson, is listed at the same address, 644 River Avenue. The same directory, and the one for 1962, also lists a Mrs. Eugenie Erickson at 107 Rugby Street; whether that is the same woman is not proven.

Constance kept working. The Warwick directories for 1963 and 1964 list her as the widow of Laurence B. Douglas, a nurse at Briarcliff Convalescent Home, living at 119 Phillips Avenue. In 1965 the directory gives her work as Briarcliffe Health Center in Johnston. She went on to spend eight years at Cranston General Hospital.

Her mother died in May 1966. The cemetery records her under a later married name, Eugenie Erickson, and she was buried in lot 84 at Saint Ann, with her own mother and her son. Constance retired in 1974.

chapters.label: Chapter 14
chapters.title: Sixth Street
chapters.html:
In her later years Constance lived on Sixth Street in East Greenwich and belonged to St. Francis de Sales parish.

She died on April 12, 1994, at eighty-one. She was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston, in section 5, lot 84, the lot where her grandmother Julia had been buried in 1931, where her mother, her brother and Laurence already lay.
